title: ReNU SYNDROME
alt_titles: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, BRAIN ANOMALIES, DISTINCTIVE FACIES, AND ABSENT LANGUAGE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ReNU syndrome (RENU) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RNU4-2 gene (620823) on chromosome 12q24.31.

paragraphs.text: ReNU syndrome is a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Chen et al. (2024) reported that all characterized individuals had moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Most walked, but late, and most were nonverbal. Nearly all had dysmorphic facial features, including a myopathic face, deep-set eyes, large cupped ears, full lips with downturned corners, and a large or protruding tongue. The disorder is caused by variants in RNU4-2, which encodes the U4 snRNA of the major spliceosome (Greene et al., 2024).

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) identified 47 cases from 47 families in the UK 100,000 Genomes Project (100KGP) who carried rare RNU4-2 variants in the regions n.62-70 and n.73-79. Of 46 cases with phenotype coding, 91% had the term intellectual disability, 91% had neurodevelopmental delay, and 61% had motor delay. These frequencies were broadly in line with general term frequencies across intellectual disability cases. Microcephaly was present in 57% of cases, compared with 18% of other cases coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality. Other features recorded among the 46 cases included seizures (24 of 46), generalized hypotonia (18 of 46), proportionate short stature (13 of 46), drooling (6 of 46), and abnormality of the upper lip vermilion (6 of 46). Compared with other cases coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality, the terms significantly overrepresented among RNU4-2 cases were microcephaly, drooling, proportionate short stature, generalized hypotonia, seizures, and abnormality of the upper lip vermilion. No terms were significantly underrepresented.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) identified 115 individuals with neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) who carried variants in the RNU4-2 critical region. Of these, 61 were from Genomics England (60 probands and 1 sib) and 54 were from other cohorts. Detailed phenotypic information was collected for 49 individuals (21 females and 28 males; median age 10 years, range 2 to 38 years). Of these, 42 had n.64_65insT, 3 had other single-base insertions, and 4 had SNVs. All 49 had global developmental delay, and all 45 assessed had intellectual disability. All individuals had moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Most (83%) walked, but late (average 3.4 years). Speech abnormality was present in 45 of 48 individuals, and 35 of 45 were nonverbal. Abnormal gait was reported in 7 of 30. Other features included hypotonia (39 of 45), seizures (37 of 48), microcephaly (37 of 48), short stature (37 of 49), and intrauterine growth restriction (8 of 45). Behavioral issues were reported in 30 of 45 individuals, autism spectrum disorder in 21 of 44, and sleep issues in 15 of 32. Seizure onset varied, with a median of 3 years and a range from the first year of life to 10 years. Seizure types included infantile spasms, focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, febrile seizures, and status epilepticus. Brain MRI was abnormal in 41 of 45 individuals. The most frequent MRI findings were reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, and delayed myelination.

paragraphs.text: Vision issues were present in 38 of 48 individuals in the Chen et al. (2024) cohort. These included strabismus (23 of 45), nystagmus (18 of 40), optic nerve hypoplasia (8 of 37), and cortical blindness. Hearing loss was present in 10 of 46. Gastrointestinal problems included feeding difficulties (32 of 42), constipation (29 of 44), and gastroesophageal reflux (21 of 43), and 13 of 41 had a gastrostomy tube. Growth problems were reported in 30 of 43 individuals. Endocrine abnormalities, including hypothyroidism and growth hormone deficiency, were reported in 17 of 39. Bone or skeletal abnormalities were reported in 27 of 42 and included osteopenia, recurrent fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, and hip dysplasia. The authors also reported limb abnormalities (23 of 42), cutaneous abnormalities (25 of 44), dental abnormalities (17 of 43), genitourinary abnormalities (15 of 43), cardiac abnormalities (5 of 43), and drooling (7 of 46). Dysmorphic facial features were present in 45 of 48 individuals. These included a myopathic face, deep-set eyes, epicanthus, wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares, large cupped ears, full cheeks, full lips, downturned corners of the mouth, high-arched palate, and a large or protruding tongue. No significant differences were noted between males and females.

paragraphs.text: Heterozygous RNU4-2 mutations cause ReNU syndrome, and the transmission pattern is autosomal dominant. Most mutations arose de novo. In the 100KGP discovery cohort of Greene et al. (2024), 37 of 47 variants were de novo, and inheritance was unknown for the other 10 because parental genotypes were missing. One parent was mosaic for n.65A>G. In the replication collections, 19 of 26 affected probands had acquired the variant de novo, and inheritance was unknown in 6. One proband had inherited n.76C>T from an affected mother.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) performed a rare-variant burden analysis of 41,132 noncoding genes in 5,529 unrelated intellectual disability cases and 46,401 controls from the 100,000 Genomes Project. RNU4-2 showed an extremely strong dominant association (posterior probability about 1), much stronger than any other noncoding gene. Three variants had a posterior probability of pathogenicity above 0.5. The disease-associated variants clustered in 2 contiguous regions of RNU4-2 (n.62-70 and n.73-79). No unaffected participant carried a rare variant in these regions, which lay within a locus markedly depleted of variation in gnomAD. Among 47 cases from 47 families, the heterozygous variants included the single-base insertions n.64_65insT, n.64_65insG, n.65_66insT, n.68_69insA, and n.77_78insT and the substitutions n.63T-G, n.65A-G, n.67A-G, and n.76C-T. Of these 47 variants, 37 were de novo. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, arose de novo in 33 different families. In replication collections, Greene et al. (2024) identified 27 further probands with rare variants in the 2 regions, including n.64_65insT and n.76C-T. Of these probands, 25 had neurodevelopmental abnormality, 1 had abnormal brain morphology, and 1 was unaffected. RNU4-2 encodes the U4 snRNA, and before this work none of the 5 snRNAs of the major spliceosome had been implicated in a human disorder.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) studied probands with undiagnosed NDD in the Genomics England 100,000 genomes project. They found a recurrent single-base insertion in RNU4-2 (n.64_65insT) in 46 of 8,841 such probands (0.52%), and the insertion arose de novo where this could be tested. The variant was absent from 3,408 diagnosed NDD probands, 21,817 non-NDD probands, 33,122 unaffected individuals, gnomAD v4.0, and All of Us, and was seen in only 1 UK Biobank individual. Overall, Chen et al. (2024) identified heterozygous variants in an 18-bp critical region of RNU4-2 (nucleotides 62-79) in 115 individuals with NDD. Most (77.4%) carried n.64_65insT. Another insertion, n.77_78insT, was seen in 6 individuals, including 2 affected sibs. Other variants included n.64_65insG, n.68_69insA, n.65A-G, n.76C-T, and n.78A-C. Single-base insertions in the region were strongly enriched in undiagnosed NDD probands compared with UK Biobank participants (OR = 1,531), and SNVs at the ends of the region were modestly enriched. In blood RNA-seq from 5 individuals with RNU4-2 variants, the authors found significantly more abnormal use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites than in controls. They also tested 27 other snRNA genes expressed in the brain. None of these genes, nor any constrained subregion, was significantly enriched for de novo or recessive variants in undiagnosed NDD probands. RNU12 showed a nominal recessive enrichment that was not significant after multiple-testing correction.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) found that the critical region maps to the T-loop (quasi pseudoknot) and stem III of the U4/U6 duplex. This region is loaded into the BRR2 helicase active site and is thought to position the U6 ACAGAGA sequence to receive the 5-prime splice site during spliceosome activation. In blood RNA-seq from 5 individuals with RNU4-2 variants, abnormal use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites was significantly more frequent than in controls (mean 8.8 vs 0.7 events). The sites used more often had more T at position +3 and more C at positions +4 and +5. These positions pair with the U6 ACAGAGA sequence, which indicates disrupted 5-prime splice-site recognition. RNU4-2 lies next to its paralog RNU4-1 on chromosome 12. Both genes are 141 bp long and differ by only 4 nucleotides. RNU4-2 was consistently expressed at higher levels than RNU4-1 in the developing human prefrontal cortex and showed much stronger chromatin accessibility in prenatal prefrontal cortex. These findings support RNU4-2 as the main U4 transcript in the brain.
